<reason>A genuinely high-level exchange. A built a sharp "security is a balance, not a box" case and landed real hits: the escalation-goes-beyond-the-motion catch, the inertia-consistency attack, and a brilliant salience judo turning B's own quiet/loud framework against default rates. But B's core route to victory survived more intact. A conceded that no deduction touches zero and that a deduction does "directly, less" for the never-enrolled, leaving B's extensive-margin mechanism (enrollment + match capture + decades of compounding) standing. Meanwhile B's two structural critiques of deductions — regressivity and asset shifting — were never squarely rebutted; A asserted price elasticity and relocated the target population rather than answering the relabeling point. B also answered both pressure questions directly and substantively (match arithmetic for the bare policy; a coherent salience distinction for the inertia charge), and B's match-beats-card-interest math defused A's debt-harm scenario, which A never returned to. A's clipped Rebuttal 2 was a small additional execution cost. B ends with the cleaner comparative: when the household does nothing, only one policy still acts.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2: answering A's scope pressure with bare-policy match arithmetic (a 3% default plus match beats the zero counterfactual at scale) and neutralizing the indebted-household harm with the instant 50–100% match beating card interest — while the salience distinction (quiet enrollment vs. loud debt) answered the inertia contradiction. A's counter-flip ("PRO's salience distinction is mine") was the debate's best single move, but it only won the intensive-margin skirmish, not the war over households who never act at all.</best_rebuttal>
